title: Short Stuff: Labor Day
summary: Short Stuff episode on the origins of Labor Day in the United States. Josh and Chuck discuss why the holiday's name seems odd, its roots in labor unions, the Peter and Matthew McGuire claims, the first Labor Day parade in New York in 1882, the push for an eight-hour day, and how President Grover Cleveland signed the federal holiday law after the 1894 Pullman strike that left workers dead. They also cover May Day as the international workers' day, the tradition of not wearing white after Labor Day as a late-1800s old-money vs. new-money fashion rule, and the decline of union membership since the 1950s. The episode closes with a note on school start dates and listener contact info.

segments.title: Opening banter and why Labor Day seems odd
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the Shorty format and joke about wearing white before Labor Day. They note that the holiday's name seems strange because it is not clearly about labor, and say its origin lies in labor unions.

segments.title: Labor union origins and the McGuire claim
segments.summary: The hosts say Labor Day became a national holiday in the US and Canada around 1882 out of labor unions. Scholars credit Peter McGuire or Matthew McGuire, with Peter McGuire getting official credit. Peter McGuire was general secretary of the Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners and co-founded the American Federation of Labor.

segments.title: First Labor Day parade in New York
segments.summary: The first Labor Day was held on September 5, 1882, in New York as a parade. Workers then often labored 12 to 14 hours a day, seven days a week. Organizers wanted unions to join forces politically and push for a five-day week and eight-hour days. Workers who took the day off faced the risk of losing pay, so the day was taken as a general strike.

segments.title: Grover Cleveland and the Pullman strike
segments.summary: Grover Cleveland signed the law making the first Monday in September a nationwide holiday. Cleveland was not a union supporter, and many think he did this to repair his image after sending federal troops to end a strike. That strike was the American Railway Union strike at the Pullman Company in Chicago, which turned bloody and left 34 workers dead. The hosts also note a bill that had been circulating in Congress years earlier, so the signing may have been coincidental.

segments.title: May Day and Labor Day around the world
segments.summary: Labor Day is called other names in other places and falls on different dates. May Day, on May 1, is the international workers' day, especially in Europe and China, and has been partly claimed as a communist holiday, which is one reason Americans don't celebrate it.

segments.title: White after Labor Day and union decline
segments.summary: The no-white-after-Labor-Day rule likely began in the 1880s as old-money families tried to separate themselves from new post-Civil War wealth. Today the rule is mostly a joke. The hosts also note that union membership, which was high in the 1950s, is now far lower, which may explain why Labor Day has become a last-blast end-of-summer holiday.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact info
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about school breaks and about listening on Labor Day. Josh gives the website stuff you should know dot com and the email address for contacting the show.
